records.quote: is the set of points of a plane which are at constant distance from a fixed point
records.claim: The circle is the set of points of a plane which are at constant distance from a fixed point in the same plane.

records.quote: The fixed point is called the centre of the circle
records.claim: The fixed point is called the centre of the circle and the constant distance is called the radius length.

records.quote: The circle is usually denoted by its center.
records.claim: A circle is usually denoted by its center: circle M means the circle whose center is point M.

records.quote: as in the figure opposite
records.caption: Circle with centre marked as point M, shaded light green.

records.quote: When drawing circle M in a plane, it divides the
records.text: When drawing circle M in a plane, it divides the points of the plane in to three sets of points as in the figure, and they are :

records.quote: The set of points inside the circle like points: M, D, E
records.claim: The set of points inside the circle, like points M, D, E, ...

records.quote: The set of points on the circle like points: A, B, C
records.claim: The set of points on the circle, like points A, B, C, ...

records.quote: The set of points outside the circle like points: X, Y, Z
records.claim: The set of points outside the circle, like points X, Y, Z, ...

records.quote: Surface of the circle : set of points of the circle
records.claim: Surface of the circle: the set of points of the circle ∪ the set of points inside the circle.

records.label: Example
records.quote: two concentric circles M, AB is a chord in
records.stem: In the figure opposite: two concentric circles M, AB is a chord in the larger circle intersecting the smaller circle at C and D. Prove that: AC = BD.
solution: Given: AB ∩ the smaller circle = {C, D}
records.notes: Solution continues on next page; no final answer on this page.

records.quote: two concentric circles M
records.caption: Two concentric circles with centre M; chord BA of larger circle meets smaller circle at D and C; E is the foot of the perpendicular from M to the chord (right angle at E, dotted segment). Points B, D, E, C, A in order on the chord.

records.quote: Construction : Draw ME ⊥ AB to intersect it at E
records.text: Construction: Draw $\overline{ME} \perp \overline{AB}$ to intersect it at E.

records.quote: By subtracting (2) from (1), we get:
records.text: Proof: In the larger circle $\overleftrightarrow{ME} \perp \overline{AB}$, so $EA = EB$ (1) (corollary). In the smaller circle $\overleftrightarrow{ME} \perp \overline{CD}$, so $EC = ED$ (2) (corollary). By subtracting (2) from (1), we get: $EA - EC = EB - ED$, so $AC = BD$ (Q.E.D.)
records.notes: Continuation of the proof begun on previous page; the page prints the Construction and Proof lines only.

objectives.label: Define the circle and its parts
objectives.description: Define a circle, centre, radius, and surface of a circle, and classify points as inside, on, or outside a circle.

objectives.label: Identify radii, chords and diameters
objectives.description: Identify radii, chords and diameters of a circle, and use them to compare lengths, including that the diameter is the largest chord.

objectives.label: Calculate measures using circle facts
objectives.description: Find diameter, perimeter, area and unknown angles using radius properties of a circle.

objectives.label: Use axes of symmetry of the circle
objectives.description: Recognise any line through the centre as an axis of symmetry and deduce the relations between a chord and a line through the centre.

objectives.label: Apply the chord corollaries to solve and prove
objectives.description: Use the perpendicular from the centre to a chord to find lengths, angles and areas, and to prove equalities and parallelism.
